items.title: Airstrikes on Iran Missile Sites May Shed Light on Justification for Dams
items.summary: Environmentalists have long puzzled over a wide network of water projects lacking any obvious justification. Then their areas were targeted in airstrikes.
items.full_text: Environmentalists have long been mystified by the significant proliferation of dams and water transfer projects like pipelines and tunnels across Iran, especially in regions that had no apparent need for them. Some analysts think they now know the answer after U.S. and Israeli airstrikes on concealed Iranian missile sites this year targeted many of the same areas. These analysts have concluded that the water projects may have been developed to support the country’s military buildup. Given the secrecy surrounding Iran’s missile program, any connection between it and Iran’s ambitious, decades-old initiative to develop water infrastructure remains speculative. But some experts find the evidence highly suggestive. Nima Shokri, an expert on water security, and his team at the Hamburg University of Technology, in Germany, had for years tracked an unusually high number of dams across Iran — at least 533 of them, among the most of any country in the region. “It was always puzzling to me,” he said. “Why were they building so many dams?” In the spring, Dr. Shokri was perusing news about the war in his home country when he came across a map plotting airstrikes that had targeted suspected secret Iranian missile sites. The pattern — a semicircle of dots from north to south — nearly matched that of his own map marking the locations of dams. His old question, he said, was superseded by a new one: “Why does it seem that wherever we have dams, there is a missile strike close by?” Thank you for your patience while we verify access. items.title: Pope Endures Grueling Travel in South America Weeks After Surgery
items.summary: When doctors operated on Pope Leo XIV’s lung in October, some wondered if he’d postpone a long-planned trip to South America. It’s gone well so far.
items.full_text: Flying with Pope Leo XIV over the Andes, halfway through the pontiff’s 12-day trip to South America, the journalists traveling at the back of the plane suspected something was amiss. They had expected the pope to come out from behind the business-class curtain and take questions, as he had on previous papal flights. Instead, Vatican officials abruptly told the press corps that the pope would not be speaking with them on the nearly five-hour flight from Argentina to Peru. Was the pope, who had been diagnosed with lung cancer less than a month earlier, feeling ill? Was he too exhausted to talk? Was he taking a nap? “It’s evident he’s well,” said Maria Montserrat Alvarado, who heads the Vatican’s communications department, when asked why the pope wasn’t taking questions. “He’s running circles around us.” It was perhaps inevitable that Leo’s every action on this journey, so soon after surgery to remove a lobe of his right lung, would be scrutinized for signs of fatigue or illness, particularly as the Vatican is not known for its transparency . The three-country trip, which began in Uruguay and concludes in Peru on Monday, involves a grueling schedule of 12 flights, two helicopter rides, nine Masses, 36 speeches and numerous meetings with local bishops and community members. items.title: Bahrain Convicts Dozens of Shiite Clerics in Sweeping Terrorism Trial
items.summary: The defendants were accused of colluding with Iran. Rights groups said the case raised concerns about religious persecution in Bahrain, which is ruled by a Sunni monarchy.
items.full_text: Bahrain sentenced dozens of Shiite Muslim clerics and other religious figures to life in prison on terrorism charges on Monday, accusing them of colluding with Iran against the Bahraini government. The convictions underscored rising sectarian and political tensions in Bahrain, a Gulf Arab country, amid the U.S.-Israeli war on Shiite-led Iran. Human rights groups had denounced the trial , saying that it was marred by allegations of torture and coerced confessions. A lawyer for several of the defendants said that all of them had pleaded not guilty. He spoke on the condition of anonymity, fearing retribution from Bahrain’s authoritarian government, and he described the trial as farcical, saying that lawyers had been deprived of basic information about the charges against their clients. In a statement published by Bahrain’s state news agency, the public prosecution department said that the defendants had been afforded all of their legal rights and given “a fair and equitable trial.” The statement said that the defendants had formed a “terrorist group” linked to the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps of Iran. The department accused the defendants of working to undermine the Bahraini government and said that the group’s leaders had received “assignments and instructions” from Iranian officials. “They had also sought to change the system of government by force and unlawful means through incitement to commit terrorist acts, acts of rioting and sabotage,” the statement added. items.title: Winter Nightmare Looms Early in Ukraine as Russia Strikes Relentlessly
items.summary: Even as it talks peace, Russia has opened a bombing campaign intended to strip Kyiv and other cities of heat, running water and sanitation this winter.
items.full_text: When American-led talks to end the war in Ukraine resumed last week in Abu Dhabi , the overriding question was whether Russia intended to give any ground after a nine-month lull in negotiations. But Russian missiles and drones had already done the talking for Moscow, analysts said . Weeks earlier than expected, Russia has opened an intense bombing campaign against the infrastructure that keeps Ukrainians alive and functioning in the winter. Daily waves of strikes against Ukraine’s energy system have raised fears that the capital, Kyiv, a city of three million people, could become all but uninhabitable in the coming months. In the Abu Dhabi talks, an emboldened Russia outlined hard-line demands that stood little chance of gaining acceptance by Ukraine and its European allies. That unbending stance indicated that Russia had no real interest in discussing peace now, because Moscow believes that the winter bombing campaign will strengthen its negotiating position entering the spring. “They want to come to the table holding our energy system hostage,” President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine said after a recent Russian attack. The Abu Dhabi talks will be followed by a meeting on Thursday between President Trump, President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia and the Chinese leader, Xi Jinping, at a summit in Shenzhen, China. It was unclear whether the three leaders would discuss the war in Ukraine. Assaulting infrastructure has become Moscow’s strategy for victory as it has failed for nearly five years to achieve its major objectives in Ukraine. While Russia has tried each winter to knock out the country’s power system and freeze its people into submission, Ukrainian cities are now in their most precarious position of the war. The grid is more fragile after years of strikes, and the Ukrainian military is struggling to protect the system because of dwindling air defenses. Thank you for your patience while we verify access. items.title: What to Know About Trump’s Trip to Asia
items.summary: President Trump will also meet with regional leaders, including Australia’s prime minister, who said “we want to see a de-escalation in the conflicts.”
items.full_text: President Trump sets off this week for meetings in Asia that will culminate in a summit with two strongmen he has often praised: President Xi Jinping of China and President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia. It will be the first time the three men, who command the world’s largest nuclear arsenals, will have sat down together. Mr. Trump plans to discuss the reduction of nuclear weapons in the world and the war against Iran, according to a White House spokeswoman. He is not expected to bring up Russia’s war with Ukraine. Mr. Trump will travel first to Manila, then to southern China, and will meet with regional leaders confronting an array of uncertainties. Those include the course of the war between the United States and Iran, high energy prices and mounting concern over the risks of artificial intelligence. For Mr. Trump, the trip will be a pivot to foreign policy and relationships after American voters delivered a swift rebuke to his party in the midterm elections. His trip also comes as his administration faces scrutiny over a scandal involving the former chief executive of Nvidia, the tech giant, which has raised questions about Chinese espionage and American tech exports. Echoes of Yalta The highlight of Mr. Trump’s trip is expected to be his meeting with Mr. Xi and Mr. Putin on Thursday in China. The prospect of their summit has drawn comparisons to the 1945 conference in the Crimean city of Yalta, where the leaders of the United States, the Soviet Union and Britain met to decide the shape of postwar Europe. items.title: South Korea to Examine How K-Pop Industry Treats Underage Performers
items.summary: The announcement came after a New York Times investigation about the restrictive contracts of the group NewJeans, signed when its members were 14 to 17.
items.full_text: South Korea’s government is planning to study how the K-pop industry treats underage performers, who are central to the industry, and to re-examine the standard template for contracts it released nearly two decades ago. The Ministry of Culture, Sports and Tourism will start an industrywide survey sometime next year, a ministry official said in a telephone interview on Monday. The government already studies the K-pop industry, checking whether record companies follow its standard contract and how much money is invested in training young stars. The new effort will focus specifically on how underage artists are treated, but its methodology, scope and exact timeline have not been decided on. The announcement came just over a week after The New York Times published an investigation into the record contracts signed by the members of NewJeans, one of K-pop’s biggest girl groups, when they were ages 14 to 17. The investigation found that the contracts removed language included in the government template that guarantees rights for minors, such as the rights to education and sleep. It was a rare look into the business of K-pop, which has long been dogged by allegations of exploitation . Record companies recruit children who are aspiring stars, put them through years of intensive training and then often bill them for those costs. Several stars have died by suicide . Two years ago, NewJeans tried to quit their label in a dispute that turned into one of K-pop’s most public fights, with the members saying they had been mistreated. A court later held them to the contracts they had signed, which run until 2029. The Seoul Broadcasting System reported the ministry’s plan earlier. In 2009 , after a boy band sued its label over restrictive work agreements, the authorities created a standard contract. It outlined protections such as capping agreements at seven years, taking into consideration an artist’s physical and mental well-being and transferring trademark rights to the artist after the terms end. The template has been amended several times over the years but still largely remains legally nonbinding. Record companies often alter clauses and add their own conditions. Some do not use the template at all, a government survey found.

items.title: They Defeated a Strongman. But Can They Run a Country?
items.summary: Serbia’s student movement was deliberately leaderless and made group decisions to unseat Aleksandar Vucic. Now no one seems quite sure what happens next.
items.full_text: They had no leader, no political party and no conventional campaign. They made decisions by raising their hands after hours of debate in university classrooms, a slow and cumbersome process billed as a unique experiment in direct democracy. That free-form approach to politics of Serbia’s students proved so effective that, in a general election on Oct. 25, they achieved what established opposition parties had failed to accomplish for more than a decade: routing the well-oiled political machine of Serbia’s strongman leader, Aleksandar Vucic. Mr. Vucic, nearing the end of his second term as president and barred from running again, had resigned as president a month before the October vote for a new Parliament, gambling that his governing party would win and that he could keep his grip on power by becoming prime minister. He had held that post twice before. His plan was upended by the election victory of a slate of parliamentary candidates selected by students in freewheeling campus meetings. Their selections and electoral successes marked the culmination of a striking exercise in collective decision making. That approach, some believe, could hold lessons for democratic movements beyond Serbia. But the principles that carried the students to victory may not, on their own, be enough to build a functioning, coherent and durable government. The diverse list of candidates chosen by the students, nearly all political novices with a wide range of sometimes contradictory views, reflected a belief that everyone should have a say in a leaderless movement united by the single objective of getting rid of Mr. Vucic and the system he created. items.title: Searching for the Last Stoats of Waiheke Island
items.summary: Can the tourist destination become the first urban island to rid itself of the stoat — an introduced predator that has ravaged New Zealand’s endemic wildlife?
items.full_text: To catch a stoat, you need to think like one. For Tilde Sorensen, that means imagining having tiny legs and picturing which route the weasel-like creature might take as it haunts the wilderness of New Zealand, preying on unique birdlife. Then she sets up a trap along that path. “We’ve caught all of the ones that will happily go into a trap. So now we’ve got to figure out how to get the really shy ones,” Ms. Sorensen said of the stoat population on Waiheke Island, a 40-minute boat ride from New Zealand’s largest city, Auckland. “We’re trying to work ourselves out of a job.” Ms. Sorensen is a stoat-detect-and-respond coordinator for a project called Te Korowai o Waiheke , a Māori name that means The Cloak of Waiheke. It has captured more than 280 stoats since 2020 and, while it is not known how many remain, testing suggests the population has dwindled. The campaign to eradicate stoats, and many other introduced species, has widespread support in New Zealand, where introduced predators, including rats and possums, kill about 25 million native birds each year . Waiheke Island, which covers about 36 square miles, is home to 4,300 people, a number that swells to about 45,000 in the summer. Thank you for your patience while we verify access. items.title: Canada’s Leader, Once a Curiosity at Asia Summits, Is Now a Star
items.summary: Prime Minister Mark Carney is courting Europe, but the bigger payoff might be in China, where he will share summit stages with Xi Jinping, Vladimir Putin and President Trump.
items.full_text: The importance of Europe to Prime Minister Mark Carney’s plan to diversify Canada’s economy and politics away from its reliance on the United States was underscored last week by his travel schedule. Mr. Carney added a stop in Dublin, joining a meeting of European leaders before the start of a previously planned trip to Asia. Last month Mr. Carney announced that Canada is officially seeking to become the first “ associate member ” of the European Union. But experts say that Asia offers the greater economic opportunity. “Prime Minister Carney certainly seems to have a strong focus on Europe, which gives an impression that he is not looking toward Asia,” said Kazuto Suzuki, a professor at the University of Tokyo’s graduate school of public policy. “Nevertheless, if Canada is to avoid dependence on the U.S. market and form a coalition of middle powers, cooperation with Asia is essential.” Last year, Mr. Carney was something of a curiosity at the meetings of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations and the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum. But his speech in January at the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, and President Trump’s addition of energy security threats to his trade war with the world have made Mr. Carney and his energy-rich country a marquee attraction at both.

items.title: International Students Are Turning Away From U.S. Universities
items.summary: For a second year, Trump administration policies appear to be scaring away international students, disrupting the finances of the American colleges that depend on them.
items.full_text: The enrollment of new international students at American universities dropped once again this fall, fueled by deep uncertainty about visas and job prospects. A survey released Monday found that new international student enrollment plunged by 15 percent, a figure that was particularly worrisome for higher education executives following a precipitous 18 percent decrease last year. Including preexisting students, international student enrollment declined 9 percent this fall, according to the survey, adding to last year’s drop of 3 percent. For years, American colleges and universities had attracted growing numbers of international students, who often paid full tuition, indirectly subsidizing tuition for domestic students. But President Trump’s crackdown on immigrants, which has occasionally swept up foreign students, along with confusing visa policies and a trade war with China, one of the top suppliers of international students, have stoked fears that the United States is no longer a welcoming place to study. Ted Mitchell, president of the American Council on Education, a large education trade organization, characterized the combined two-year downturn as “likely historic,” noting that international students had been a growth sector for higher education. He pointed to departures among international students who were already enrolled as a worrying sign. “These are people who’ve already started, and they’ve said, ‘No, the risk is too high. I’m not going back,’” Dr. Mitchell said. Thank you for your patience while we verify access. If you are in Reader mode please exit and log into your Times account, or subscribe for all of The Times. items.title: Is Jensen Huang Plotting a Comeback?
items.summary: Prominent figures in Silicon Valley want to see Jensen Huang reinstalled as Nvidia’s boss. Some in the Trump administration don’t want him to return.
items.full_text: Andrew here. The Jensen Huang –Nvidia tale has escalated into a high-stakes tug of war. On one side, Elon Musk and other Silicon Valley figures are mounting a pressure campaign to reinstate Huang as C.E.O. But Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has called for a “dramatic shake-up” and an outside replacement, citing concerns that Nvidia may have bypassed export laws by selling chips to Chinese-linked intermediaries. (Adding a new wrinkle, Megaspeed said on Sunday that Alice Huang , the Chinese executive at the center of the scandal, left the firm in August 2025.) What happens next is anyone’s guess. The former Nvidia chief is expected to testify before Congress in the coming weeks. But the ultimate showdown may happen overseas: President Trump is heading to China to meet President Xi Jinping , where this topic is almost certain to come up. Or is it? More below. A Huang comeback? It’s been four days since Jensen Huang resigned as the C.E.O. of Nvidia, after news reports said he had an affair with Alice Huang , the data center executive U.S. intelligence officials believe was a Chinese spy. (He also had an affair with a direct subordinate, The Times has reported.) Now, some of Silicon Valley’s biggest heavyweights want to reinstate Huang, even as some Trump administration officials called for new blood atop the chip maker at the center of the artificial intelligence boom. Yet there are signs that President Trump himself may not raise the issue even as he prepares to meet with Xi Jinping , China’s top leader. Huang is reportedly on board with efforts to bring him back, The Financial Times reported on Sunday, citing unnamed sources. Ever since he resigned, many in Silicon Valley have wondered whether he would lead a comeback, much as Sam Altman did after briefly being ousted from OpenAI nearly three years ago. items.title: As Phillips Scales Back, the ‘Big Two’ Auction Houses Seem to Stand Alone
items.summary: Phillips was always an underdog in the auction world, but it had ambition to compete with Christie’s and Sotheby’s. Then the economics changed.
items.full_text: Two works in this week’s marquee auction at Phillips — a loosely brushed group portrait by David Hockney and a roughly hewed limestone head sculpture by Amedeo Modigliani — carry estimates above $10 million. Compare that with what’s on offer at Christie’s and Sotheby’s: a combined 45 lots above that blue-chip threshold. “One client described us as scrappers and I loved that description,” said Martin Wilson, Phillips’s chief executive. “That is how we put our sales together. We don’t get a ready-made big collection landing in our laps.” Like Sotheby’s and Christie’s, Phillips has an English pedigree planted in the 18th century, when it managed the estate sales of dead aristocrats. But in recent years, the company seems to have retreated from its centuries of competition with the “Big Two,” leaving some experts in the art market to worry about having to deal with a true duopoly. In today’s auction market, it’s expensive to sell top material. Auction houses increasingly rely on financial guarantees to win consignments, promising sellers millions of dollars before the auctioneer even picks up the gavel. They fly paintings to Paris, Taipei and Hong Kong, recruit celebrity bartenders to work their parties, and hire star architects to design their salesrooms. Wilson, who joined Phillips as a lawyer in 2018 and became chief executive in 2024, objected to the idea that the company was shying away from this kind of competition. But, he said, Phillips no longer intended to grow at all costs. “You start with growth being the priority over profitability. We had reached that point in growth where we had credibility,” he said, and it was “time really to look at profitability.” Thank you for your patience while we verify access. items.title: Doubts Loom Over a van Gogh as Auctions Aim for a $2.8 Billion Week
items.summary: Major paintings by Cézanne, Picasso and Klimt are positioned to entice collectors as Sotheby’s seeks resolution for the auction’s most coveted painting. Five bellwether works to watch.
items.full_text: The art market’s grand finale beginning Monday comes with a $2.8 billion forecast — and plenty of drama. A late-breaking claim by heirs of the Jewish former owner of a van Gogh landscape has challenged a Sotheby’s auction Wednesday of a painting of blossoming chestnut trees, which was expected to sell for about $180 million. The heirs, in an email to the auction house from their lawyer that was shared with The New York Times, said that the canvas was originally sold under Nazi-era duress in 1936, and that they were “prepared to work toward a fair and just solution.” The high-stakes clash underscores how heavily the three major auction houses are betting on tradition at the New York fall marquee sales of contemporary and modern art. Counting the van Gogh, they are estimating they will sell about $600 million more than last November, when one collector brought a shimmering Klimt portrait home for over $236 million, making it the second-most expensive painting ever auctioned. Experts said the new estimates reflected a surge in high-value works and signs of confidence in the buying appetites of the ultrawealthy, despite the potential for rising interest rates and recent stock market wobbles. “There’s been a lot of wealth created since Covid, and there’s still a tremendous appetite this fall for top-quality material that’s fresh to market,” said Liz Sterling, a partner at the New York- and Palm Beach-based advisory firm Sterling Teel Capital. items.title: How Sam Bankman-Fried Lost Out on a $35 Billion Jackpot From Anthropic
items.summary: The founder of the collapsed FTX crypto exchange, who is serving prison time for fraud, would have made a windfall from a $500 million investment in Anthropic.
items.full_text: Sam Bankman-Fried, the convicted cryptocurrency fraudster, lives in a 30-person unit at the federal prison in Lompoc, Calif., a barbed-wire compound about a million miles away from his former life as a technology billionaire in the Bahamas. For the most part, Mr. Bankman-Fried, 34, tries not to think about all the “could-have-beens,” he said on a recent call. But one has become difficult to ignore. In late 2021, the heyday of his FTX crypto exchange, Mr. Bankman-Fried spent $500 million on a 13.5 percent stake in a little-known artificial intelligence start-up called Anthropic. This week, Anthropic is set for an initial public offering that is expected to value the company at $1.4 trillion, potentially one of the largest Wall Street debuts in history. At that valuation, Mr. Bankman-Fried’s investment, diluted over several years, would now be worth an eye-watering $35 billion — about the size of FTX’s entire business at its peak. But the shares are gone. They were tied up in bankruptcy court until 2024, when executives overseeing the scattered remains of FTX sold the Anthropic stake for $1.34 billion — a tiny fraction of its current value. For Anthropic, the fate of those shares is an odd quirk of history. For Mr. Bankman-Fried, it’s a source of extreme frustration and resentment. Even after a fraud conviction, a failed appeal and a succession of public humiliations, he is still trying to prove his innocence, arguing that FTX had sufficient resources to avoid bankruptcy. items.title: A Classic Car Show From Paris Aims to Turn Heads in Manhattan
items.summary: Retromobile will feature vehicles from Jerry Seinfeld and Billy Joel and a parade of famous models from bygone eras — and some newer classics, too.
items.full_text: It began as a humble car gathering in a dilapidated former train station in Paris, where hobbyists scoured for flea-market parts. Fifty years later, Retromobile has grown into a bucket-list destination for car lovers: an indoor colossus of collectible cars, restoration specialists, auctions and art, a market for automobilia and delightful oddities. In France, the Salon Retromobile is further known for its eclectic, egalitarian spirit, one that organizers worked to translate to its inaugural show outside Paris, at the Jacob K. Javits Convention Center in Manhattan running Thursday to Sunday. “Automobiles are in the American blood,” said Gerard Neveu, Retromobile’s chief executive. “And New York is the big stage, so we will begin with a splash.” The splash includes models from two quintessential New Yorkers. While Jerry Seinfeld drove a Saab 900 on his sitcom, he is also known for owning one of the world’s most historically significant Porsche collections. Four special cars from the Seinfeld Collection will be among those displayed from roughly 200 exhibitors. These include a revolutionary 1955 Porsche 550 Spyder, the brand’s first purpose-built racecar. A Gooding Christie’s auction will feature more than 70 motorcycles from Billy Joel’s collection, with proceeds benefiting the Joel Foundation. A 1978 Triumph Bonneville T140 with a painted piano-key gas tank was a gift from Madison Square Garden in honor of Joel’s 150th sold-out show. That Triumph is expected to fetch $10,000 to $15,000. items.title: Apple Was Late to the Video Podcast Boom. Now It’s Trying to Catch Up.
items.summary: They will soon be free to all Apple TV users and will appear on more than one billion devices that have the app, including Rokus and smart TVs.
items.full_text: Apple helped turbocharge the rise of podcasts two decades ago, but as video podcasts reshape the industry it’s fallen behind competitors like YouTube and Spotify. Now it’s playing catch up. On Monday, Apple will add a video podcasts section to Apple TV, initially just for testing with developers. They will soon be free to all users even if they don’t pay for Apple’s streaming service and will appear on over one billion devices that have the Apple TV app, including Rokus and smart TVs. Apple also plans to increase the number of video podcasts on its regular Podcasts app, where it introduced video features nine months ago but has been working to bring some of the biggest shows on board. “We want podcasts to be available wherever people want to enjoy them — the small screens, big screens,” said Oliver Schusser, a vice president at Apple who oversees services including podcasts, television and music. “It’s really about discovery and helping the creators to reach a new audience. We didn’t approach this in a way that would financially benefit us.” Video podcasts have proliferated in the past few years as audio creators adapted their shows to reach consumers spending more time on video platforms like YouTube. The video format has proved attractive to celebrities, including Amy Poehler, Pete Davidson and Food Network’s Ina Garten . And the trend of “clipping” — creating short buzzy video clips from longer shows to post on social media platforms like TikTok and Instagram — has encouraged creators to add video to their podcasts. The popularity of video podcasts, driven by YouTube and Spotify, and newer entrants like Hulu and Netflix, has pushed Apple down in the podcast platform rankings. Spotify passed Apple as the top platform among weekly podcast consumers in the United States at the end of 2022, according to survey data from Edison Research at SSRS. YouTube took over the top spot at the end of 2024. In Edison Research’s third-quarter survey, YouTube remained the most popular, followed by Spotify then Apple Podcasts. Netflix was No. 7. Many in the industry had long awaited Apple’s move. “It’s super smart that they’ve done it, but it’s after a lot of people in the space wanted them to make it available,” said Megan Lazovick, a vice president at Edison Research. items.title: A Bull Market, Fueled by Pikachu, Charizard and Nostalgia
items.summary: On the 30th anniversary of the franchise, Pokémon cards are skyrocketing in value — to the point that collecting them isn’t just big business, it’s a viable livelihood.
items.full_text: Scott Pratte turned his boyhood hobby into his livelihood. But he doesn’t usually tell people he’s a Pokémon card collector. In conversations, he is vague about what he does for a living, saying his business involves collectibles or investments. “I wouldn’t want to share numbers on the record,” Mr. Pratte, 39, said in an interview, though he noted that the past few years have been “million-dollar years in earnings.” Pokémon originated as a pair of video games released in Japan for Nintendo’s Game Boy console in 1996. The franchise expanded to include a trading card game, released the same year, which came to the United States in 1999. That’s when Mr. Pratte and others first marveled at the artwork, swapped cards on playgrounds and obsessed over completing sets they shrouded in plastic sleeves in protective binders. As Pokémon has grown — on its 30th anniversary, the franchise now spans TV shows and films, all manner of merchandise and a stable of more than 1,000 “pocket monsters” — the cards have skyrocketed in value.

items.title: Billions in Insurance Money Is Being Bet on AI Debt, and Analyst Are Nervous
items.summary: Insurance companies are investing billions of their customers’ money into A.I. deals as analysts warn of mounting risks.
items.full_text: When Elon Musk needed help financing a large purchase of artificial intelligence chips earlier this year, Wall Street offered an elegant solution. Mr. Musk and his team of advisers created a financial entity that would borrow billions to buy the chips and then lease them back to xAI, his artificial intelligence effort. This way, xAI wasn’t technically the borrower, which helped make its official debt load look smaller to investors. To help fund this complicated arrangement, $2.4 billion of the debt was sold to an insurance company called Athene, which manages life insurance policies and annuities for retirees, according to a Moody’s Ratings report. The deal was part of an increasingly popular playbook: tapping insurance companies, which are historically among the most cautious investors, to make loans to tech titans like Mr. Musk and further fuel the A.I. boom. The amount of A.I. debt being held by insurance companies has soared this year. U.S. life insurers, including some of the largest like Athene and Corebridge Financial, held $85.2 billion in A.I. debt as of June 30, up 24 percent from six months prior, according to Moody’s. While this accounts for just 2.1 percent of life insurers’ total debt, their exposure is expected to grow quickly. Life insurers could hold up to $185 billion of A.I. investments by the end of next year, according to Moody’s. Thank you for your patience while we verify access. items.title: Trump’s Plan for A.I. Supremacy Fuels Resistance in the Philippines
items.summary: A planned American-led artificial intelligence hub in the Philippines has sparked fierce opposition over concerns about displacement, resources and threats to national sovereignty.
items.full_text: In May, Roseller Rodriguez, a mayor in the Philippines, was startled to learn from news reports that American officials had arrived in his district to start an artificial intelligence hub. He saw a video of senior American and Filipino officials standing on a makeshift stage, unveiling a new initiative called Pax Silica. Mr. Rodriguez had not been invited. Nor had he ever heard about the hub. Was it a data center? Where would the water and electricity come from? What would happen to the farmers living there? Months later, he says he has few answers. “I’m not concerned with the geopolitics of Pax Silica,” Mr. Rodriguez said in his office in the municipality of Capas. “My problem is Pax Silica will be built in our community.” Last December, the United States started Pax Silica to unite partners around A.I. supply chains independent of China. The initiative is part of President Trump’s effort to counter Beijing’s economic and technological influence. Trump administration officials have cast it as a 21st-century successor to “Pax Americana,” the era of relative peace among major powers after World War II. items.title: How Jensen Huang’s Secret Led to His Downfall at Nvidia
items.summary: Nvidia’s leader said his relationship with a female customer was just about business. But what he was concealing eventually led to his resignation from the company he created.
items.full_text: Jensen Huang was agitated. It was September 2025, and The New York Times had just called his company about a Singaporean data center firm called Megaspeed that had been led by a Chinese woman named Alice Huang, or Huang Le. The Times was reporting that Mr. Huang, the chief executive of the chip maker Nvidia, had a close relationship with her. Mr. Huang, who Nvidia employees say could have a volcanic temper, wanted to know what The Times was insinuating. Though he didn’t deny that he knew the woman, he was bothered by the suggestion that they might be close, people familiar with the discussion said. Nvidia mounted an aggressive defense. Madison Huang, Mr. Huang’s daughter who acted as her father’s chief of staff, pressed the company’s communications team to push back forcefully. They also had reinforcements, a crisis communications firm called Heller. They insisted that Mr. Huang and the woman from Megaspeed just had a business relationship. Over the next 13 months, Mr. Huang stuck with his story, even after The Times reported last month that the U.S. had gathered intelligence showing that Ms. Huang was secretly working with China’s top spy agency. But last weekend, facing new revelations about the relationship, Mr. Huang finally came clean to Nvidia’s general counsel. He had been having an affair with the woman, after all, said the people familiar with the discussions. The relationship with the Megaspeed executive wasn’t Mr. Huang’s only secret. On Wednesday, a Times reporter called Mr. Huang to ask him about a second extramarital relationship. This time, it was an affair with an executive who reported to him. items.title: The Jensen Huang Scandal Has Shocked Even Scandal-Prone Silicon Valley
items.summary: As Jensen Huang abruptly departs, the tech community grapples with an eternal question: Why do the smartest and most successful men so often act so stupidly?
items.full_text: Artificial intelligence promises transcendence. We will ditch our tired and inefficient bodies, say farewell to tedious work and trips to the grocery store. The computer will tend to all human needs and solve all human problems. Well, that was the idea. A.I. was supposed to achieve a new level of reality this month with the public sale of shares of Anthropic, one of the two start-ups that have created and defined this young industry. A trillion-dollar company will be born, yielding billionaires galore. A.I. is the biggest Silicon Valley story ever. But last Sunday it was suddenly pushed aside when the chief executive of the company whose chips are literally powering this intelligence revolution confessed to cheating on his wife with a woman, Alice Huang, who U.S. officials believe was spying for China. By Thursday morning he had resigned, something few thought possible just days earlier. The scandal that took down Nvidia chief Jensen Huang is full of implications for national security and the global A.I. boom. Mr. Huang ranked among Mark Zuckerberg, Steve Jobs, Elon Musk and Bill Gates as tech leaders who were considered by the world to be inseparable from the companies they built. In Silicon Valley, people were mostly just stunned by the news. Those who have been around for a long time, and seen the stretch of territory south of San Francisco evolve from hardware manufacturing to software development to the dot-com frenzy and now the A.I. boom, said they had never seen anything like it. Tech veterans have witnessed amazing ascensions and equally abrupt falls. They have seen abundant arrogance. Fortunes made and fortunes lost in an instant. But there’s something that stands out this time: Transcendence was never supposed to be tawdry. Thank you for your patience while we verify access. items.title: Tech Leaders Rally Behind Jensen Huang
items.summary: In social media posts and letters to Nvidia’s board, Mr. Huang’s billionaire peers described him as a singular leader who could not be replaced at Nvidia.
items.full_text: Many of Silicon Valley’s executives and investors are rallying behind Jensen Huang, who resigned as Nvidia’s chief executive on Thursday after revelations that he had affairs with an employee and with a woman whom U.S. officials believed to be a spy for China . In social media posts and letters to Nvidia’s board of directors, Mr. Huang’s billionaire peers described him as a singular leader who could not be replaced at Nvidia. Mr. Huang’s exit, they argued, would set the United States back in the artificial intelligence race. And they blamed Nvidia’s board for bowing to pressure. “Jensen drove supply chain brilliantly at Nvidia, but many of those deals were a handshake with Jensen, not a written contract,” Elon Musk, SpaceX’s chief executive and the richest person in the world, said in a social media post on Saturday. “Without Jensen, at least some of those critical deals will be lost.” The support put a spotlight on Nvidia’s role as the linchpin of the A.I. boom and on Mr. Huang’s leadership as the company grew into one of the most valuable in the world. Nvidia, which started making computer chips for video games, now controls an estimated 90 percent of the market for the advanced chips used in the big A.I. projects that are driving the U.S. economy. Along the way, Mr. Huang became Silicon Valley’s consummate dealmaker , turning Nvidia into a central banker for start-ups that needed chips and funding. “We believe the board should avoid a rush to replace Jensen that undermines and thwarts the best interests of shareholders,” Brad Gerstner, the chief executive of Altimeter Capital Management, and Gavin Baker, the chief investment officer of Atreides Management, wrote in a letter sent on Friday. The investors, whose firms are Nvidia shareholders, asked the company’s board to consider “all options on the table, including the potential return of Jensen Huang.” An open letter to Nvidia’s board , titled “Stand With Jensen,” asked the board to reinstall Mr. Huang as chief executive, to conduct an independent investigation and to explain its actions. As of Saturday morning, the letter had nearly 100,000 signatures, including by current and former employees of Nvidia, business partners like Mr. Musk, and start-up leaders and shareholders including Garry Tan, the chief executive of the venture capital firm Y Combinator. items.title: Inside Microsoft’s Rush to Get Back Online After a Global Outage
items.summary: A prolonged outage left many without email and other services, the most recent reminder that the world’s technological underpinnings rely on just a few companies.
items.full_text: Late into the night Thursday, hundreds of Microsoft engineers and top executives were sitting in their darkened offices or home basements, logged into a video conference triaging a nightmare scenario for a technology company. The world still runs on email, and much of that is processed through Microsoft Outlook. For hours, a company outage affected hospitals, schools, businesses and Congressional offices in Washington. Even Microsoft’s own staff couldn’t use email. On the videoconference, Scott Guthrie, the senior most executive overseeing the company’s computing infrastructure, was proposing possible fixes, according to a person familiar with the call who was not authorized to speak publicly. People chewed on fingernails, rubbed their foreheads and debated how to turn off other services to prevent a “stampeding herd” so that as systems come back online, they would not be overwhelmed with new demands and shut back down. By Friday morning, the company had apologized at least twice. It said it determined that the problem stemmed from a recent upgrade to its network, which shut down some servers, and that the systems were steadily improving. “Given the scale of demand, we restored services gradually, validating stability at each stage,” the company said in a statement. “While this took longer, it helped ensure a stable restoration.” Finally, they had kept the herd at bay. The prolonged and widespread outage was just the most recent reminder that the technological underpinnings of modern life and business are run through just a handful of major companies. And while cyberattacks and malicious actors can target their systems, sometimes the companies learn the hard way that they can introduce devastating flaws when updating or maintaining their own global systems. Hospitals, law enforcement and government agencies and other vital services are often left vulnerable — unable to function for hours or days at a time. items.title: Trump Administration Moves to Close A.I. Chip Loophole Ahead of China Trip
items.summary: The rules, a topic of fierce debate in the administration, could cut back on Nvidia’s sales to foreign data centers serving Chinese companies.
items.full_text: The Trump administration said on Monday that it was moving forward with a new rule that would clamp down on China’s ability to access advanced A.I. chips through the use of data centers outside China’s borders. The rule aims to close what many in Washington see as a loophole that has allowed China to sidestep a Commerce Department ban that prevents Chinese firms from buying the most advanced A.I. chips made by companies like Nvidia. China’s ability to continue accessing the chips by renting them from data centers in Southeast Asian countries and elsewhere has been a significant source of contention within the Trump administration. The new rule establishes restrictions for overseas data centers that supply “significant volumes of computing power” to firms with headquarters in a small group of high-risk countries, a list that includes China, Russia and Iran. Data centers are also required to perform due diligence on their customers. The provision, which goes into effect in 90 days, will “undermine” the ability of companies in those countries from using U.S. chips to train advanced A.I. models, the release said. It will also require a license to export advanced chips to companies with headquarters in Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand or Brazil, which have a higher than normal risk of smuggling, the administration said. The plan to restrict that loophole comes just days before President Trump is scheduled to travel to China for an economic summit, where he will also meet with the Chinese leader, Xi Jinping. The share prices of major chip makers, including Nvidia, Intel, Broadcom, Micron, AMD and others, fell sharply in premarket trading on Monday. Thank you for your patience while we verify access. items.title: Fan Fiction Site AO3 Returns, and So Do Its Readers, in Droves
items.summary: The archive, which is home to tales inspired by the likes of “Harry Potter” and “Heated Rivalry,” was taken down more than two weeks ago, leaving its fans bereft.
items.full_text: It’s a library of nearly 19 million works, more than double the circulating materials of the New York Public Library, so when it was knocked offline in a “security incident” more than two weeks ago, its 12 million users were aghast. The volunteers who run the fan fiction site AO3, short for “ Archive of Our Own ,” had quickly assured its enormous community that no data — especially all those works — had been lost and that it would be restored in four weeks. But on Sunday, the repository of homespun stories based on works like “Harry Potter,” “Twilight” and “Heated Rivalry” was mostly back online, with some features — like importing external work — temporarily disabled, to help the site return earlier than expected. “The intensity of the response speaks to how deeply fan fiction has become woven into our lives,” Dana Bryce , a writer and cultural commentator in Toronto, said on Sunday afternoon. “The AO3 outage has shown how deeply participatory storytelling is now embedded in everyday cultural life,” Ms. Bryce said. “And its absence made the importance of that relationship visible.” The works hosted on the nonprofit, noncommercial archive are inspired by books, films and even celebrities, like the members of K-pop bands. It is run entirely by volunteers, and operated by the Organization for Transformative Works. “Modern audiences are voracious,” Ms. Bryce said. “We want more, always. And nowhere is that more true than in stories. We are increasingly dissatisfied with the finality of the close of novels, television series and films. Stories have become worlds that audiences want to revisit indefinitely.” She said that fan fiction democratizes storytelling, and that AO3 readers were not limited by long publishing cycles or a single author’s pen. “It’s a shared experience,” she said. “Instead of reading in silos, audiences can read and write as a collective, reimagining, revising, reinterpreting and expanding fictional worlds, becoming active participants in storytelling.” AO3 said on Sunday that it would not disclose what had happened to the site, referring to the outage as a “security incident.” It said it would not share specifics of mitigating changes it was putting in place but did say it was consulting with a security firm. It recommended that users change their passwords, while noting that “we have no reason to believe that the user database was compromised.” There was so much site traffic on Sunday that some users faced delays loading it. “This is an intentional measure to help manage traffic,” AO3 said. Ms. Bryce was not surprised by readers’ response on Sunday, calling AO3 “a collective cultural archive.” “It’s a living record of evolving audience desires and attachments,” she said.

items.title: Microsoft’s Global Outage and Fixes: What We Know
items.summary: Disruptions to the company’s email, messaging and other products lasted about 36 hours, hampering companies and services around the world.
items.full_text: Microsoft said early Saturday that it had fully restored its services after a global outage disrupted them for a day and a half, hampering communications and work at schools, government agencies and offices around the world. The problems began on Thursday and cascaded around the world. The company, based in Redmond, Wash., gradually restored service through Friday until declaring an end to one of its most extensive outages of recent times in an update on Saturday around 1 a.m. Eastern time. Here’s what to know. What happened? Outages started disrupting Microsoft tools and apps around noon Eastern time on Thursday and quickly spread to more than 70 countries and territories, affecting millions of users, according to Downdetector , an outage-tracking site. Some of Microsoft’s most popular products, including the email manager Outlook, the workplace messaging and video calling app Teams and the artificial intelligence assistant Copilot, stopped working. Was this a cyberattack? Microsoft said in a statement on Friday that “for now, we can confirm that there is no indication this is the result of malicious or cyber activity.” It added that the problem was “a technical issue not related to cyber or A.I.” agents. Was the F.A.A. ground stop linked to Microsoft? The company said it had no indication that a Federal Aviation Administration ground stop issued late Friday afternoon , which has affected air travel nationwide, was related to the outage. items.title: Jensen Huang’s Resignation From Nvidia Worries the A.I. Start-Up World
items.summary: Mr. Huang championed start-ups, with Nvidia holding $48 billion worth of stakes in 229 private companies, including OpenAI and Anthropic, at the end of July.
items.full_text: For years, Jensen Huang was a frequent presence at Silicon Valley start-up events, networking with founders, judging pitch competitions and showing up at “demo” days. The Nvidia chief executive became a godlike figure in the start-up ecosystem, not just because the industry idolized him as one of the world’s most successful entrepreneurs. Mr. Huang, 63, also made it his mission to help start-ups gain a foothold against the industry’s biggest and most powerful tech companies, providing funding and computing power. “As many good ideas as we have, you don’t have all the world’s good ideas,” he said on the Acquired podcast in 2023. So Mr. Huang’s abrupt resignation from Nvidia on Thursday has investors and start-up founders nervous that they have lost a powerful ally. “Nvidia is the central bank of A.I. and all of a sudden, the Fed chairman is out,” said Tomasz Tunguz, an investor at Theory Ventures, which funds young start-ups. Nvidia held $48 billion worth of stakes in 229 private companies, including large stakes in OpenAI and Anthropic, at the end of July, according to securities filings. It more than doubled its start-up investments in six months. Thank you for your patience while we verify access.
